claims.text: CoCrFeNiMo0.85 can be deposited as a coating on a 316L stainless-steel substrate.
Cold spraying CoCrFeNiMo0.85 at approximately 3 MPa and 400°C in ambient atmosphere is a suitable processing route for damaged 316L.
Pre-surface roughening improves adhesion of the cold-sprayed HEA coating to 316L.
The proposed cold-spray process will produce a dense CoCrFeNiMo0.85 surface layer.
The proposed cold-spray process will produce a fine-grained CoCrFeNiMo0.85 surface layer.
The cold-sprayed CoCrFeNiMo0.85 layer will be metallurgically bonded to 316L.
High-velocity particle impact induces severe plastic deformation in the deposited particles and substrate surface.
Cold spraying avoids melting both the substrate and coating.
Avoiding melting prevents the thermal stresses and phase changes responsible for hot cracking.
High-velocity impact refines the coating grain structure.
High-velocity impact promotes mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding at the coating-substrate interface.
The cold-sprayed coating will have significantly higher hardness than fusion-weld-repaired and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed coating will have better wear resistance than fusion-weld-repaired and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed coating will have better corrosion resistance than fusion-weld-repaired and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed CoCrFeNiMo0.85 repair will show fewer hot cracks than a traditional fusion-weld repair on 316L.
The cold-sprayed repair will show fewer hot cracks than the untreated damaged surface.
Optimization of cold-spray parameters and pretreatment will ensure robust interfacial adhesion.
Fusion-welded repairs on 316L typically perform poorly in aggressive environments because of hot cracking.
An untreated damaged 316L surface has low hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance.
Extreme geometries or damage that compromises the bonding interface may prevent the predicted coating performance.
